content: The majority of individuals with epilepsy have a favorable prognosis, with their seizures being effectively managed by a single antiepileptic drug. However, between 20% and 30% of patients, depending on the study population, develop drug-resistant epilepsy, particularly those with focal-onset seizures. Topiramate, an antiepileptic drug first introduced in 1996, has been evaluated as an add-on therapy for drug-resistant focal epilepsy. This review updates prior Cochrane Reviews from 1999 and 2014, focusing on the efficacy and tolerability of topiramate in this context. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness and safety of topiramate as an adjunctive treatment for individuals with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. A comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Register of Studies, MEDLINE, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, was conducted on July 2, 2018. No language restrictions were applied. Additionally, manufacturers of topiramate and researchers in the field were contacted to identify ongoing or unpublished studies. The review included randomized, placebo-controlled trials that evaluated topiramate as an add-on therapy in patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. Data were independently extracted by two reviewers, and outcomes assessed included the proportion of participants achieving a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency, seizure freedom, treatment withdrawal for any reason, and adverse effects. Analyses were conducted on an intention-to-treat basis, with risk ratios (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) calculated. Dose-response relationships were analyzed using regression models, and the risk of bias for each study was assessed using the Cochrane tool. The overall certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. A total of 12 trials involving 1650 participants were included. The baseline phases of these studies ranged from 4 to 12 weeks, while the double-blind treatment phases lasted between 11 and 19 weeks. The addition of topiramate to existing treatment regimens was associated with a significantly higher likelihood of achieving a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency compared to placebo (RR 2.71, 95% CI 2.05 to 3.59; high-certainty evidence). Dose-response analysis revealed that higher doses of topiramate were associated with greater efficacy, with an odds ratio (OR) of 1.45 (95% CI 1.28 to 1.64; P < 0.001) per 200 mg/day increase in dosage. The likelihood of achieving complete seizure freedom was also significantly higher with topiramate compared to placebo (RR 3.67, 95% CI 1.79 to 7.54; moderate-certainty evidence). However, treatment withdrawal rates were significantly higher in the topiramate group compared to placebo (RR 2.37, 95% CI 1.66 to 3.37; high-certainty evidence), indicating tolerability issues. Adverse effects were more common with topiramate and included ataxia (RR 2.29, 99% CI 1.10 to 4.77), concentration difficulties (RR 7.81, 99% CI 2.08 to 29.29; moderate-certainty evidence), dizziness (RR 1.52, 99% CI 1.07 to 2.16), fatigue (RR 2.08, 99% CI 1.37 to 3.15), paraesthesia (RR 3.65, 99% CI 1.58 to 8.39; moderate-certainty evidence), somnolence (RR 2.44, 99% CI 1.61 to 3.68), abnormal thinking (RR 5.70, 99% CI 2.26 to 14.38; high-certainty evidence), and weight loss (RR 3.99, 99% CI 1.82 to 8.72; low-certainty evidence). Evidence of publication bias was detected for the primary outcome (Egger test, P = 0.001). The included studies were assessed as having either low or unclear risk of bias. The overall certainty of evidence was rated as moderate to high, with limitations due to publication bias, statistical heterogeneity, and imprecision, although these were partially offset by the large effect sizes observed. In conclusion, topiramate is an effective add-on therapy for drug-resistant focal epilepsy, being nearly three times more effective than placebo in reducing seizure frequency. However, the trials reviewed were of relatively short duration, and no evidence was available regarding the long-term efficacy of topiramate. Short-term use of topiramate was associated with several adverse effects. These findings are primarily applicable to adult populations, as only one study included pediatric participants. Future research should focus on further exploring the dose-response relationship and the long-term effects of topiramate.
